nameStory: The sweet potato gets its name from its surprisingly sweet-tasting underground tubers, which set it apart from regular potatoes with their sugary, almost dessert-like flavor. Despite the name similarity, sweet potatoes and regular potatoes are only distant cousins in the plant world – the 'sweet' part is what really defines this tropical vine that somehow made its way to New England gardens.
description: Sweet potato is a sprawling, vining plant that belongs to the morning glory family, though you might not recognize it as a relative of those familiar funnel-shaped flowers. The plant produces heart-shaped leaves on long, trailing stems that can spread several feet across the ground or climb up supports. While famous for its edible orange tubers underground, in New England you're most likely to encounter sweet potato as an ornamental 'potato vine' cascading from hanging baskets or covering garden beds with its lush, colorful foliage.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped to lobed leaves that feel smooth and slightly waxy to the touch, ranging from bright green to deep purple or bronze depending on the variety. The leaves alternate along the vine and often have a subtle sheen that catches sunlight.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Long, trailing vines that spread horizontally across the ground or cascade downward, with stems that feel soft and somewhat succulent when squeezed gently. The vines can root at nodes where they touch soil.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Funnel-shaped flowers similar to morning glories, typically white to pale pink with a darker throat, though flowering is rare in New England's climate. When present, flowers are about 1-2 inches across and open in morning hours.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth, green to reddish stems that feel tender and break easily when bent, often developing roots at joints where they contact moist soil. The stems have a slightly milky sap when broken.

habitat: In New England, sweet potato is almost exclusively found in cultivated settings like gardens, container plantings, and landscaped areas, as it cannot survive our winters outdoors. You'll spot it in sunny garden beds, hanging baskets, and as groundcover in annual flower displays. It thrives in well-drained, fertile soil and full sun locations, often planted alongside other heat-loving annuals.

seasonality.spring: Young plants appear in gardens after the last frost, typically late May or early June, with bright green heart-shaped leaves just beginning to trail.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with lush, spreading vines and fully developed colorful foliage. This is when sweet potato vines are most vigorous and recognizable in New England gardens.
seasonality.fall: Foliage may change color or begin to decline with cooler temperatures, and any tubers underground would be harvested before first frost in cultivation.
seasonality.winter: Not present outdoors in New England – the plant dies with the first hard frost, though it may survive indoors as a houseplant in sunny windows.

funFact: Sweet potatoes are more closely related to morning glories than to regular potatoes – in fact, you can actually eat sweet potato leaves as nutritious greens, just like you might eat spinach or kale, and they're considered a delicacy in many parts of the world!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other ornamental vines like common morning glory, but sweet potato leaves are consistently heart-shaped and more substantial feeling, while morning glories have thinner leaves that are often more deeply lobed. Sweet potato vines also lack the twisting tendrils that morning glories use for climbing.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'potato,' sweet potatoes are completely different plants from regular potatoes – they're not even in the same plant family! In many parts of the U.S., sweet potatoes are confusingly called 'yams,' but true yams are yet another unrelated plant entirely. This naming confusion dates back to enslaved Africans who called sweet potatoes 'yams' because they resembled the true yams from their homeland.
compareHints: Unlike its morning glory relatives that are primarily grown for their showy trumpet flowers, sweet potato is grown for foliage and edible tubers, rarely flowering in New England's climate. While other Ipomoea species like common morning glory have thin, papery leaves, sweet potato leaves are thicker and more substantial with a waxy feel. Sweet potato also tends to spread horizontally rather than climb vertically like most of its morning glory cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common morning-glory has the largest flowers among New England's morning-glories, with those distinctive heart-shaped leaves that lack the three-lobed structure of ivy-leaved morning-glory.

Among New England morning-glories, ivy-leaved is distinguished by its three-lobed leaves - common morning-glory has unlobed heart-shaped leaves, while white morning-glory has much smaller flowers and often heart-shaped but sometimes three-lobed leaves.

Garden Morning Glory stands out from its Ipomoea cousins with its large flower size and vibrant blue color range - Common Morning Glory has smaller, more purple-pink flowers, while Ivy-leaved Morning Glory has distinctly lobed leaves rather than the simple heart shape.
Cypress vine is instantly distinguished from all other morning glories by its incredibly fine, thread-like leaf segments - every other morning glory in New England has broad, solid leaves.

Among its morning glory relatives, moonflower stands out for its exclusively nighttime blooming and pure white color - most other Ipomoea species bloom during the day in shades of purple, blue, pink, or red.
Red morning glory stands out from other New England morning glories primarily by its small size and brilliant red color - most others have much larger purple, blue, or white flowers.
Among New England morning-glories, wild potato vine stands out with its pure white flowers that have pink throats, while most others have purple, blue, or pink flowers.

Among New England morning glories, scarlet creeper is the only one with consistently bright red flowers - common morning glory has purple flowers, ivy-leaved morning glory has blue to purple blooms, and moonflower has large white flowers.

White morning-glory stands out from its Ipomoea relatives by having the smallest flowers in the genus - much tinier than the dinner-plate-sized blooms of moonflower or the vibrant purple trumpets of common morning-glory.
